doc.title: Marty Morell interviewed by Monk Rowe, Orlando, Florida, February 24, 2017

title: Trio conversation versus accompaniment
summary: Evans's early trio made the rhythm section a conversation, and Morell's busy brushes follow that.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: And did you try to play verbatim?
No. I don’t remember from one day to the next what I played the last time.
But you — the recordings I picked out to listen to, I’m not sure how to say this. You like to double things up a lot or frequently.
Double things up by for instance, that piece it seems like you could have been playing – you were fairly busy on the snare drum with the brushes. I guess that’s what I mean.
Right, right. Well that’s kind of what I hear, and that’s very stylistic, Bill Evans’ style.
And it’s a conversation rather than an accompaniment.

You know what I mean? It’s kind of a conversation rather than just – and that’s basically like that early trio with Scott LaFaro, Paul Motian and Bill, they created a whole new © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-

rhythm section kind of style, right? Where they were three musicians having a conversation rather than the bass and the drummer accompanying the piano player. Right? So that’s where the door started opening for the role of the drummer and the bass player, the interaction in the rhythm section.
I like that because it sounded like a ballad and an uptempo tune at the same time to me.
Well yeah. That’s a beautiful piece of music. That’s Claus Ogerman.
